# Rehearse a job interview by letting Copilot play the hiring manager

> **In short:** You can turn Copilot into a mock interviewer in about five minutes: tell it the job, the company, and the questions you fear, then answer out loud and ask for blunt feedback on what to improve. It will not replace a real coach, but it can drill you until your answers feel natural.

Practicing interview answers in your head almost never works. You forget half of what you wanted to say, miss the small details, and never get the honest feedback that turns a shaky answer into a confident one. Copilot, Microsoft's AI assistant, can act as the hiring manager asking you questions, follow up on weak spots, and tell you, in plain words, what to say differently. This guide shows you how to set that up from scratch, even if you have never opened Copilot before.

## Before you start

- A **Microsoft account** (the same one you might use for Outlook, OneDrive, or Xbox). You can sign up for free at the official Microsoft account page if you do not have one.
- A **device with a browser** — laptop, desktop, tablet, or phone. You can also use the Copilot app on iOS or Android if you prefer typing on your phone.
- A **target job description** (a real posting you are applying to is best). Copy and paste it somewhere you can find it quickly. Have a notebook or a blank document open too, for typing out your answers.
- About **30 minutes** for the first full run. After that, a single 10-minute round is enough to warm up before a real interview.
- A free Copilot account covers the basics. Some advanced features, like longer voice conversations, may sit behind a paid Microsoft 365 Copilot plan. We will flag where that matters.

## Step 1 — Open Copilot and start a fresh conversation

In your browser, go to the **Copilot homepage** and sign in with your Microsoft account. Once the chat page loads, look for a button or icon labeled **"New chat"** or **"New thread"** — usually at the top of the left-hand sidebar, sometimes shown as a small pencil or plus symbol. Click it so you begin with an empty conversation rather than an old one.

💬 Example: type **"Hi, I want to practice for a job interview."**

You'll know it worked when a clean chat box appears with no previous messages, and Copilot greets you in a friendly tone.

## Step 2 — Hand Copilot the job description and your background

Paste the full job posting into the chat, then add a short note about you: your current role, years of experience, and the kind of company you are interviewing with. After the paste, ask Copilot to take on the role of the hiring manager for that specific job. This context is what makes its questions feel real instead of generic. Without it, you will just get the same five questions every beginner gets.

💬 Example: *"Here is the job description for a [Job Title] at [Company]. I have [X] years of experience in [field]. Please act as the hiring manager for this role and interview me one question at a time. Wait for my answer before moving to the next question."*

You'll know it worked when Copilot confirms the role it is playing and asks you the first question rather than starting with small talk or a long explanation.

## Step 3 — Answer the first question out loud or in writing

Treat this like a real interview: do not skip straight to the feedback. Pick **one of two modes** and stay in it for at least three questions before switching. In **typed mode**, write your answer in the chat box the way you would say it, then send. In **voice mode**, tap the **microphone icon** in the chat area and speak naturally; your words show up as text on screen as you talk. Speaking out loud is harder, and that is exactly why it helps.

💬 Example: if the first question is *"Tell me about a time you handled a difficult customer,"* answer with a real story using the classic structure: Situation, Task, Action, Result. Keep it under two minutes.

You'll know it worked when Copilot acknowledges your answer, asks a thoughtful follow-up, or moves on to the next question — proof that it understood what you said.

## Step 4 — Ask for honest, specific feedback on your answers

Once you have answered two or three questions, pause the role-play and ask Copilot to switch back to coach mode. Request feedback on what you said: what was clear, what was vague, what filler words or rambling you should cut, and which stories came across strongest. Be specific in your ask. The more pointed your request, the more useful the reply.

💬 Example: *"Stop the interview for a moment. Look at my last three answers. Tell me: (1) which stories were strongest and why, (2) where I rambled or repeated myself, (3) one concrete sentence I should rewrite in my next answer."*

You'll know it worked when Copilot gives you a short, organized critique with at least one sentence you can rewrite right away. If the feedback feels vague, ask it to be more specific — that usually unlocks better detail.

## Step 5 — Restart the interview and apply what you learned

Click **"New chat"** again to wipe the conversation and start fresh. This time, give Copilot the same job description but add a short line about what you want to do differently this round: stronger openings, fewer filler words, or a clearer story about a specific skill. Then answer the first question again. You will feel the difference within a minute, and that feeling is the whole point of rehearsing.

💬 Example: *"Let's do this again for the same [Job Title] role. This time, I want my answers to start with the result, then explain how I got there. Please push me if I ramble."*

You'll know it worked when your second answer comes out tighter than the first, and you can name one thing you changed on purpose.

## Common mistakes

- **Skipping the job description.** Without the real posting, Copilot asks the same generic questions everyone has heard a hundred times. Paste the actual text — it takes 30 seconds and changes everything.
- **Asking for feedback too soon.** If you ask "how am I doing?" after a single answer, you get thin feedback. Answer at least three questions first, then ask for a critique, so Copilot has something real to compare.
- **Letting Copilot answer for you.** It is tempting to ask "what should I have said?" — but that just produces a perfect answer you cannot deliver under pressure. Ask for **what to fix in your own words**, then try again.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** the same rehearsal trick works for salary negotiations, parent-teacher meetings, or any conversation you have been dreading. Practicing the actual words out loud removes most of the anxiety.
- **For your business or work:** if you manage or hire people, you can use this method to coach teammates who freeze in interviews. Share the prompt from Step 2 and let them practice on their own time.
- **If you're just getting started:** do one short round tonight, even 10 minutes. The first answer will feel rough, and that is the point. By the third answer, you will already sound calmer.

## Try it now

Open Copilot, paste the job description you are preparing for, and answer just one question out loud. Do not aim for perfect — aim for *finished*. You can always run it back tomorrow.
